title: How Do You Disciple One Person at a Time?
subtitle: The recovery of one-to-one disciple-making through ordinary spiritual friendship, over coffee, on a walk, in unhurried conversation across years. Not a program and not mere friendship, but a friend who intentionally walks one other person toward Christ. What Scripture, the old soul-friend traditions, and honest research say about the slow work of forming a person, and how an ordinary believer with no title can begin to walk someone toward Jesus this week.

connections.label: Friendship is the ground this grows in. Before you walk someone toward Jesus, you have to be a friend who stays.
The table is the other room where one-to-one discipleship happens. Coffee and a meal are the same instinct.
You cannot walk someone toward a Jesus you are not following yourself. The walk starts with your own.
The first people you will ever disciple one to one are likely under your own roof. The home is the first classroom.
Where the church's whole vision of forming people gets its shape. The pathway every spiritual friendship plugs into.

parts.title: The Friend You Were Never Discipled By
parts.body:
Somewhere in your years of faith, you were probably told to find a mentor. A wiser Christian, a few rungs up, who would meet with you and pour into you and answer the questions you were too embarrassed to raise on a Sunday. Maybe you looked. Maybe you even asked someone, and it was awkward, and it fizzled after the second coffee because neither of you knew what it was supposed to be. And maybe you have carried, quietly, the sense that you missed something, that there was a kind of formation other people got and you did not, a Paul to your Timothy who never showed up.

Now reverse it. You are older in the faith than you were. Younger believers are around you, a new Christian still wobbling, a college kid home for the summer with real doubts, a coworker who started asking about church, a son who is somewhere between curious and gone. And you have never once thought of yourself as the kind of person who disciples another person, because that word has a uniform on it. It belongs to the staff, the trained, the gifted, the ones with a curriculum and a system and a confidence you do not feel. So you watch these people from a careful distance and assume someone more qualified will walk with them, and usually no one does.

This is the strange gap at the center of the church. We believe in spiritual fathers and mothers, in older men teaching younger men and older women younger women, in the chain of faithful people who entrust what they have heard to others who will teach still others. We believe it, and almost none of us are doing it, one to one, with a name and a face. The chain has thinned to a thread. Most Christians have never been discipled by a person, only by sermons, and have never discipled a person, only attended things. We have a great deal of content and very few fathers.

The reason is not that we do not care. It is that we have confused two things that the old church kept distinct. We have friends, the people we relax with, who never call us higher. And we imagine mentoring, a formal, intimidating thing with a structure we do not have. We have lost the middle, the thing the ancients called a soul friend, a friend who is also going somewhere, who walks beside you toward Christ and is honest enough to say the hard thing on the way. Not a program. Not a casual buddy. A friend with a direction.

Let me say the thing plainly, the way I wish someone had said it to me. You do not need a title, a curriculum, or a gift you were not given. You need one person, a standing cup of coffee or a regular walk, an open Bible now and then, the nerve to ask a real question, and years. That is not a watered-down version of disciple-making. It is the oldest version there is. It is how Paul made Timothy and how the faith has crossed every generation since, one friendship at a time, and you can begin it this week.

parts.title: Why One Person Beats a Thousand
parts.body:
The stakes start with a quiet arithmetic the church keeps getting wrong. We are impressed by the room. We measure ministry by how many are in the seats, and we pour our best energy into the gathering of crowds, on the unexamined assumption that the bigger the audience, the bigger the impact. But a person is not formed by being in a large room. A person is formed by being known in a small one. The crowd produces attenders. The one-to-one friendship produces disciples, and Jesus, who could draw five thousand, spent the overwhelming bulk of his three years on twelve men and a great deal of it on three. He was not bad at scale. He understood it better than we do.

It matters because formation travels through relationship or it does not travel. You can learn information from a stranger across a room. You cannot learn a way of life that way, the things that actually change a person, how to pray when God is silent, how to forgive a betrayal, how to hold a marriage together, how to handle money and anger and ambition like someone who belongs to Jesus. Those are caught, not taught, watched in a real life at close range over time. A sermon can plant a conviction. Only a friend who lets you see how he actually lives can show you what the conviction looks like on a Tuesday, in traffic, under pressure, when no one is applauding.

It matters because the questions that decide a person's faith are almost never asked in public. The doubt that would unravel a believer, the sin he cannot stop, the wound she has never told anyone, the question she is afraid is too dangerous to say out loud in a church, these surface only in the safety of a single trusted friendship, over the third coffee, on the long walk, when it is just the two of you and there is no audience to perform for. A church can run flawless services for a decade and never once get near the real interior of a soul. A friend can get there in a season, because the friend is allowed in the room where the person actually lives.

And it matters more in a post-Christian America than it has in living memory, because the old delivery system is failing. For generations the faith was passed down by sheer cultural momentum, a Christian-ish society that did half the discipling for us, family Bibles and a default of churchgoing and a moral air everyone breathed. That air is gone. The young believer now lives in a world actively pulling the other way, and information from a platform is no match for it. What still works, what has always worked, is a flesh-and-blood friend who is further down the road and willing to walk beside, the one form of witness a skeptical age still trusts, because it cannot be faked across a screen.

Finally it matters because it is the only thing that multiplies. A person formed in a crowd learns that faith requires a crowd, an expert, a building, a production he could never mount himself, and the chain ends with him. But a person walked toward Jesus by an ordinary friend learns that discipleship requires only what he already has, a life, a Bible, a willingness to walk with one other person, and so he turns and does the same. One becomes two becomes four. The whole math of the kingdom hides inside a single unglamorous friendship that decided to go somewhere.

parts.title: Paul, Timothy, and the Pattern of the One
parts.body:
Open the New Testament and look for the crowds, and you find them. But look for how anyone actually became like Christ, and you find pairs. You find Paul and Timothy, a relationship the letters treat as the most natural and central thing in the world. Paul calls him my true child in the faith, my beloved child, and writes to him not as a project but as a son, recalling the tears, the shared sufferings, the years on the road. You followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, Paul writes, and the list is not a syllabus. It is a life laid open and watched. Timothy did not take Paul's course. Timothy traveled with Paul, was discipled by proximity, and became a father to others in turn.

And notice the command Paul gives him, because it is the engine of the whole thing. What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. Count the generations in that one sentence. Paul, to Timothy, to faithful men, to others also. Four links, and the method holding the chain together is not a program but a person handing the deposit to a person, who hands it on again. This is the architecture of how the faith was always meant to move, not broadcast but entrusted, hand to hand, friend to friend, down the centuries to whoever is reading this now.

Paul was himself discipled this way. Before there was Paul and Timothy there was Barnabas and Saul, and the order of those names matters. When the newly converted Saul was feared by everyone and trusted by no one, it was Barnabas, the son of encouragement, who took him, vouched for him, brought him in, and then went and found him in Tarsus when there was kingdom work to do. Barnabas walked beside a dangerous, difficult, brilliant new believer until that believer could stand, and the church got Paul because one man was willing to befriend him first. Every Timothy is downstream of a Barnabas. No one disciples who was not first discipled.

Then look at Jesus, and look at the shape, not just the teaching. He had the crowds, and he had the seventy, and he had the twelve, and inside the twelve he had Peter, James, and John, and inside the three he had the one, the disciple whom he loved, who leaned against him at the supper. He took the three up the mountain at the transfiguration and into the garden at Gethsemane, the highest moment and the lowest, and he wanted his closest friends near for both. The Son of God, with infinite love available and the salvation of the world to accomplish, structured his ministry as a series of narrowing circles, and he did not apologize for it. He appointed the twelve, Mark says, so that they might be with him. Being with him was the curriculum. The classroom was the road.

And the word he finally gave that friendship is the deepest word in the book. No longer do I call you servants, he said, for the servant does not know what his master is doing, but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. There it is, the thing we keep splitting apart, friendship and discipleship, fused in a single sentence. To disciple, in the mouth of Jesus, is to befriend, and to befriend is to disclose, to make known what you have received from the Father. The Christian who walks a friend toward Christ is not inventing a technique. He is doing the most ancient thing the faith knows, the thing Jesus did with John, the thing Paul did with Timothy, the thing the gospel itself is, a God who came near, walked beside, opened his heart, and called us friends.

parts.title: The Soul Friend and the Long Tradition
parts.body:
The church has a word for the friend who walks you toward God, and it is older than most of our denominations. In the Celtic Christianity of Ireland and Scotland, the figure was called the anamchara, the soul friend, the one to whom you opened your heart, confessed your sin, and bared your inner life so that another could see what you could not see alone. Brigid of Kildare, in the sixth century, is remembered for the bracing proverb that a person without a soul friend is like a body without a head. The early Celtic church did not treat such a friendship as a luxury for the spiritually advanced. It treated it as a basic organ of a living faith, the head on the body, without which the rest could not see where it was going.

Six centuries later a Cistercian abbot gave the idea its greatest book. Aelred of Rievaulx, writing around the year 1160 in a Yorkshire monastery, composed Spiritual Friendship, still the deepest Christian treatment of the subject ever written. Aelred took the friendships that filled his own life, real, warm, particular affections for particular monks, and refused to treat them as a distraction from holiness. He argued the opposite, that a true spiritual friendship is a school of love in which two souls help each other toward God, that Christ is the unseen third in every such friendship, and that friendship begun in this life runs on into the friendship of heaven. A friend, he wrote, is one to whom you can pour out your heart, before whom you can lay your soul bare, and with whom you can go to Christ. He dared to set John's own words over the whole enterprise, that the one who abides in this kind of love abides in God.

The Reformation and its heirs kept the practice while changing its setting. The English and American Puritans developed what they called conference, the deliberate, searching spiritual conversation between believers, a friend speaking to a friend about the actual state of the soul, where God seemed near or absent, where sin had gained ground, where grace had broken through. It was discipleship by conversation, ordinary believers watching over one another's souls in talk that refused to stay on the surface. Out of the same impulse came the great tradition of spiritual direction, the practice of sitting regularly with a wiser, prayerful person who helps you notice what God is doing in your life and where you are resisting him, a tradition that ran from the desert fathers through Ignatius and on into the present, always built on the same conviction, that the soul is rarely well discerned alone.

The Wesleyan revival turned the practice into a movement. John Wesley, in the eighteenth century, gathered his people into bands and class meetings, small groups and pairs that met not to study a topic but to ask one another a question that would terrify most modern Christians, how is it with your soul. They confessed sin to one another, gave account of their walk, watched over one another in love, and the result was not a lecture series but a transformed nation. Beneath the famous preaching, the real engine of early Methodism was thousands of ordinary people in small, honest, watching friendships, holding one another to Christ.

The verdict of the whole long tradition is consistent and quietly damning of our moment. The faith has never been chiefly sustained by audiences. It has been sustained by soul friends, by the anamchara and the spiritual director and the band partner and the conference, by the unspectacular, repeated, honest conversation of one believer with another about the things that matter most. We did not lose this because it stopped working. We lost it because we got busy and embarrassed and impressed by size, and traded the soul friend for the seminar. The good news folded inside the indictment is that the tradition can be picked back up by anyone willing to be deliberate. The body has been wandering without its head. The head is available. It is the friend who will walk with you and ask the real question, and you can be that friend for someone this week.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The human sciences have studied mentoring, apprenticeship, behavior change, and how people actually become different over time, and a Christian can receive what they have found with gratitude and a sharp eye at once, because all truth is God's truth and none of it is the whole truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly about why one-to-one formation works, and then tests each against Scripture, because every account of how a person changes carries a hidden picture of what a person is and where the change finally comes from, and that is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.source: Situated learning and the theory of apprenticeship
secular.author: Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger
secular.whatItGetsRight: Studying how people actually acquire complex skills, Lave and Wenger showed that real competence is rarely learned in a classroom and is overwhelmingly learned through apprenticeship, by a newcomer working alongside a master inside a real community of practice, watching, imitating, attempting, being corrected, and slowly moving from the edge of the work toward its center. Knowledge that changes a person is caught in shared activity far more than it is transferred in instruction. This is a precise account of how a craft, a trade, or a way of life is genuinely passed from one person to another, and a sharp rebuke to any attempt to mass-produce mastery through information alone.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research describes the shape of formation with startling accuracy and cannot supply its source. It explains how a learner becomes like a master through shared life, and Scripture says the Master we are being conformed to is Christ and the power that conforms us is the Spirit, not merely the proximity. A person can apprentice at a godly friend's side for years and gain only good habits and warm company if the Spirit does not give the growth, for neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the increase. The science rightly recovers the relational, shared-life nature of real change. The gospel names whose life is being formed in us and who is doing the forming, and it is not the mentor.

secular.source: The research on mentoring and adult development
secular.author: Daniel Levinson and the mentoring literature
secular.whatItGetsRight: Levinson's longitudinal work on the seasons of adult life, and the broad mentoring research that followed it, found that a genuine mentor relationship is one of the most powerful developmental experiences an adult can have, often decisive for who a person becomes. The studies consistently show that the relationship matters more than any technique, that it works through trust and identification and sustained presence over years, and that its absence is a measurable loss, leaving people to figure out the hardest transitions of life with no one further down the road to walk beside them. The literature confirms that human beings are formed by being accompanied.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The mentoring research honors accompaniment and reaches the edge of its deepest meaning without crossing it. It can demonstrate that a wiser companion shapes who we become and cannot say who we were made to become or by whose pattern. Scripture supplies the missing center, that the goal of all true spiritual accompaniment is not the mentor's image but Christ's, until we all attain to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. A mentor who reproduces himself has succeeded by the world's measure and failed by heaven's. The research rightly recovers the formative power of being accompanied. The gospel insists that the friend is only ever pointing past himself, decreasing so that another may increase, lest the disciple be conformed to a man instead of to the Lord.

secular.source: The science of how habits and character actually change
secular.author: Research on behavior change and James Clear
secular.whatItGetsRight: A large body of work on behavior change has shown that lasting change is not chiefly a matter of willpower or information but of small actions repeated over time inside a supportive environment, and that the company you keep is one of the strongest predictors of who you become, because we absorb the norms of the people around us almost without noticing. We rise or fall to the level of our closest relationships. The research confirms the ancient intuition that character is contagious, that we become like those we spend our unhurried hours beside, and that change therefore travels through sustained proximity to changed people far more reliably than through resolve.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science rightly observes that we become like our company and stops short of the warning and the hope Scripture attaches to that very fact. Do not be deceived, bad company ruins good morals, Paul writes, and the same law that makes corruption contagious makes holiness so, which is why we are told to imitate those who through faith inherit the promises. But Scripture refuses to reduce sanctification to social osmosis. The change God works is not merely new habits absorbed from better company but a new heart given by the Spirit, a death and a resurrection, not a behavioral upgrade. The research recovers the power of proximity. The gospel insists the deepest change is a miracle no environment can manufacture, worked by a God who makes the dead alive.

secular.source: The research on self-disclosure and trust
secular.author: Social psychology of intimacy, after Sidney Jourard
secular.whatItGetsRight: Beginning with Jourard's work on self-disclosure and continued by decades of research on how intimacy forms, social psychology established that closeness grows through a gradual, mutual opening of the inner self, that one person going first with honesty invites the same in return, and that relationships deepen in proportion to what people are willing to let one another see. The studies confirm that hiding keeps people lonely even in company, that vulnerability is the doorway to being known, and that the trust required for any real influence is built precisely by the willingness to be honest about oneself first.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research maps the mechanism of honesty and cannot reach the healing that Scripture attaches to it. It can show that disclosure builds closeness and is silent about confession, which is disclosure aimed at God's mercy. Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed, James writes, and the promise is not merely connection but healing, a thing no psychology can dispense. The danger the research cannot guard against is honesty that opens the heart to another person and never to God, intimacy that becomes its own end, two people deeply known to each other and unforgiven. The science rightly recovers the power of going first. The gospel turns the disclosed sin toward the only One who can take it away.

secular.source: Spiritual direction and the recovery of the contemplative tradition
secular.author: Eugene Peterson and the spiritual formation movement
secular.whatItGetsRight: Peterson and a generation of writers on spiritual formation recovered, for a hurried and program-driven church, the ancient practice of the long, attentive, unhurried accompaniment of one soul by another. They named the great enemy of formation as hurry, insisted that you cannot form a person on a schedule built for production, and retrieved the conviction that the work of helping someone grow in God is slow, particular, prayerful, and personal, the patient noticing of what God is already doing in a single life. Their critique of a church addicted to size, speed, and technique is exact, and their call back to the cure of souls one at a time is a genuine recovery of something the church had nearly lost.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: This stream is the closest of the five to Scripture and still must be tested, because the recovery of slow, soul-by-soul attention can drift, in some hands, toward an inward contemplation that loses the cross and the call to repentance. Scripture keeps spiritual direction tethered to a Christ who not only accompanies but commands, who says both come to me and go and sin no more, and who sends his friends out to make disciples, not merely to be present to one another. The danger is a formation so gentle and unhurried that it never confronts, all noticing and no naming. The movement rightly recovers the patient cure of souls. The gospel keeps that cure honest, refusing to let accompaniment become a substitute for the word that wounds before it heals.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who equally believe in one-to-one discipleship still differ on how directive the spiritual friend should be, and each emphasis is guarding against a real failure it has watched ruin people. The dividing question is whether the friend who walks beside another should lead with intention and accountability, naming sin and pressing toward growth, or lead with presence and discernment, accompanying patiently and letting God set the pace. Hear each at its strongest, because the wisest soul friends hold both, and the difference is mostly one of where to lean.

views.view: The intentional friend: lead with direction and accountability
views.body: This view holds that a spiritual friendship which never names sin, never asks the hard question, and never presses toward growth has quietly stopped being discipleship and become only company. It takes seriously that Paul did not merely accompany Timothy but charged him, instructed him, corrected him, and called him toward a clear aim, that Scripture commends the faithful wounds of a friend and the iron that sharpens iron with friction included on purpose, and that we are told to exhort one another every day, that none be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. So the intentional friend brings an agenda of love to the coffee, a willingness to ask how the marriage really is, whether that habit was confessed, where God is being avoided, and to keep asking when the answer is evasive. Advocates argue that a generation of vague, undirected Christian friendship has produced warmth without growth, people endlessly accompanied and never actually changed, and that real love is willing to be temporarily unwelcome for the sake of a brother's holiness. The failure they are guarding against is a friendship so afraid of confrontation that it watches someone walk toward ruin and says nothing, mistaking cowardice for grace. They are quick to add that the intentional friend must never become the controlling one, that direction without patience and humility crushes rather than forms, and that the goal is a brother freed by truth, not a project managed by a self-appointed expert.

views.view: The patient friend: lead with presence and discernment
views.body: This view holds that a spiritual friendship which rushes to fix, correct, and manage has quietly stopped trusting God and started doing his work for him. It takes seriously that Jesus often asked rather than told, that he let people sit with their questions, that he was famously unhurried and refused to force growth on anyone's timetable, and that real transformation is the Spirit's work, which cannot be scheduled or pressured into being. So the patient friend leads with presence, walking faithfully beside another for years, listening far more than instructing, praying, noticing where God already seems to be moving, and trusting that the slow accumulation of honest companionship will bear fruit the friend could never manufacture by confrontation. Advocates argue that the church is full of eager fixers who drove people away with premature correction, that most people already know their sin and need a safe friend more than another critic, and that patient accompaniment honors both the person and the God who is actually doing the forming. The failure they are guarding against is the controlling mentor who turns a friendship into a project, names sin before trust is built, and crushes the very person he meant to help. They are quick to add that patience must never curdle into permissiveness, that a friend who never once speaks the truth in love has abandoned his post, and that real presence eventually includes the hard word, spoken late and gently, but spoken.

parts.title: What the Long Walk Forms in the One Who Walks Beside
parts.body:
You begin to walk a friend toward Jesus believing the work is for him. It is. But the long walk forms the one who walks beside at least as much as the one being walked, and this is the part no one warns you about. The moment you commit to accompany another soul toward Christ over years, God begins to use that very commitment to finish things in you that no sermon ever reached.

It forms patience, the patience that is mostly the death of your own hurry. You cannot disciple anyone quickly, and the long walk will cure you of speed or you will quit, because growth in another person runs on a clock you do not control and cannot accelerate, the slow seasons where nothing seems to move, the same struggle confessed for the third year, the question answered and asked again. You want progress you can measure, and God gives you a person instead, and in the waiting he sands the impatience out of you until you begin, slowly, to love the way he loves you, who has been patient with your same sin for decades and has not walked away.

It forms honesty, because you cannot walk someone toward a holiness you are faking. The friend you disciple watches your actual life, not your edited one, and over time the gap between your words and your walk becomes unbearable to maintain. So the friendship that was supposed to grow him quietly indicts you, exposing the prayerlessness behind your advice about prayer, the resentment behind your counsel about forgiveness, the very sins you keep helping him fight. This is not the friendship failing. It is the friendship working, driving you back to the cross you keep pointing him toward, until you realize you are not his teacher above the lesson but his fellow student a half step ahead, both of you being taught by the same Lord.

It forms a love for the particular and difficult person rather than the idea of ministry. It is easy to love the lost in general and hard to love the specific friend who relapses again, resists the obvious, takes years to grasp what you explained in an hour, and disappoints you right when you thought he had turned a corner. The long walk strips the romance off disciple-making and leaves the thing that actually saves people, the patient, particular, unspectacular love that keeps showing up to the same coffee with the same person who is not finished. You learn how impatient and proud you really are, and that learning is the friendship forming you.

And it forms a friend in the image of the Friend, until you understand the gospel from the inside. Every time you stay with someone who is slow, sinful, and hard to love, and you keep walking beside him toward Christ, you are doing in miniature exactly what Jesus did with you, who called you friend while you were still a servant, who walked beside you for years before you understood, who has never once given up on the long, slow, costly work of making you like himself. You cannot keep practicing that faithfulness without being changed by it, without the patience you are extending to another teaching you at last how patient has been the Friend who walks beside you. That is the secret hidden in the long walk. While you are spending years to make a disciple, the Lord who walked to Emmaus is quietly making one of you.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: This is the part the whole resource exists for, because spiritual friendship is not a beautiful idea to admire but a practice to begin, and almost any believer can begin it. You do not need a title, a curriculum, or a gift you were not given. You need one person, a standing time, the nerve to ask a real question, an open Bible now and then, and years. What follows is a concrete path from the first cup of coffee to a friendship that reproduces, walking one ordinary person toward Jesus over time. If your own walk with God is in a place where you cannot imagine helping anyone, start there, with a pastor or a friend who will walk with you, because no one disciples who was not first discipled, and that is not a detour from this, it is the on-ramp. Begin with one name and one invitation, this week.

steps: Pray over the actual people in your actual life and ask God for one name. Not the most promising or the most like you, but the one he keeps bringing to mind, the new believer, the doubting coworker, the wandering friend, the younger person already half-looking to you. Disciple-making one to one begins on your knees, asking the Lord of the harvest who he has already placed within your reach.

Make the ask small, honest, and free of pressure. Do not propose a program or use the word discipleship, which will scare most people off. Say something true and ordinary, like, I would love to grab coffee now and then, I have appreciated you and would enjoy getting to know you better. Keep it a friendship from the first sentence, because that is what it is.

At the first coffee, do not perform and do not preach. Ask about his life, his story, his work, his family, and listen more than you talk. Let him see you are interested in him and not in a project, and let the first conversation accomplish only one thing, that he would want to do it again. Trust is the soil everything else will grow in, and it is built by being genuinely curious about a person.

Before you part, plant the seed of a rhythm. Say something like, this was good, could we make it a regular thing. A single coffee is a nice afternoon. A standing coffee is where a person gets discipled, and the entire difference is the word regular, said out loud while it is still easy to say.

Set a fixed time and defend it like a bill that must be paid. The same person, the same coffee shop or the same walking route, every week or every other week, at an hour you both protect. Formation is the fruit of repetition over time, and the single most important decision you will make is to give this friendship a settled, defended place in your calendar that does not depend on either of you feeling inspired.

Move past small talk by asking better questions and then waiting. How is your week actually going. What is hard right now. What are you hoping for. Most people have no one who asks and stays for the answer, and the simple practice of caring questions returned week after week builds a trust that no shortcut can buy. Resist the urge to fix what he says before you have fully heard it.

Begin to share your own real life, including your walk with God, as a natural part of the conversation rather than a lesson. Talk about where God has felt near or far this week the way you talk about work or family, honestly and without performance. Let him watch an ordinary Christian be a struggling, hopeful, real human being, because that sight does more to make the faith believable than any argument you could mount.

Take note, between meetings, of where he seems to be with God and where the real questions and struggles are surfacing. You are not building a file, you are paying attention, learning this particular person so that when the time comes to open Scripture or ask the hard thing, it lands in his actual life and not a generic one. Discipleship is personal or it is nothing, and personal means you remember.

Bring the Bible into the friendship in the most natural way possible. Suggest that you read a short passage together, a few verses from a Gospel, and talk about it over the coffee you are already having. Ask three simple questions anyone can handle, what does this show us about God, what does it show us about ourselves, and what might it mean for this week. You do not need to be the expert. You need to open the book and let Jesus teach.

Add prayer to the rhythm, starting small enough that neither of you is intimidated. Ask how you can pray for him this week, write it down, and follow up next time to see what God did. Then begin to pray together, even a sentence each at the end, because praying with a friend, and watching prayers answered, disciples a person in the reality of God faster than any explanation, and it is something even a brand-new believer can begin to do.

When trust has been built, begin to be honest about sin, yours first. Go first with a real struggle of your own, because vulnerability is almost never matched until someone risks it, and let that open the door to the deeper questions, what is hard to surrender, what keeps tripping him up, what he has never told anyone. Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, James writes, that you may be healed, and healing is what you are after, not information.

Name what is happening when the moment is right. Tell him plainly that walking with Jesus is the thing your whole life is built on, and ask whether he wants to learn how to follow Jesus, or, if he already believes, whether he wants to grow on purpose with your help. The friendship has earned you the trust to say the direct thing, and love eventually says it, because a friendship that never once calls a person toward Christ has loved him too little, not too much.

From early on, hold up the truth that he will one day do this for someone else, so that reproduction is assumed and not bolted on later. Tell him plainly, one day you will walk beside someone the way we are walking, this is simply how the faith has always moved. A friend who is only ever poured into becomes a consumer, but a friend who knows he is being equipped to pour into another becomes a maker of disciples.

When he is ready, encourage him to begin walking beside someone of his own, and stay available as he does, the way Barnabas stayed near Paul. Resist the instinct to keep him dependent on you forever. The aim is not the most impressive single friendship but the most friendships, each one able to reproduce, until one coffee has multiplied into a quiet web of people walking one another toward Jesus across a church and a city.

Keep the pattern simple enough that an ordinary person can carry it without you, a regular meeting, caring questions, a short passage with the three questions, honest talk about sin, and prayer together. The reason the faith crossed every century is that its method required nothing a believer did not already have, and a pattern you can hand to anyone is a pattern that will outlive and outgrow you. Complexity does not reproduce. Simplicity does.

Stay in it for the long haul, through the seasons when the friendship is rich and the seasons when it is thin, trusting God with a harvest you cannot force. Some you walk beside will flourish and some will wander, some will turn and disciple others and some will break your heart, and your task is not to control the outcome but to keep showing up to the coffee, opening the book, and walking beside, the way Jesus walked the road to Emmaus, until the day you arrive together at the only destination that finally matters, and the long walk is over, and you see him face to face.

kicker: Spiritual Friendship and the Long Walk
